query: Reported superconducting high-entropy alloys are dominated by Nb-Ta matrices, while other studies concern titanium-rich systems based on heavy transition metals and partly ordered systems. Consequently, these precedents do not establish what controls superconductivity in high-entropy alloys outside the best-studied material classes. Within the defining constraint of a solid solution containing at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each, what governs superconducting behavior in such an uncharacterized high-entropy alloy, and why? State one testable mechanistic hypothesis, a controlled comparison against the starting material, predicted observations relative to the baseline, applicable boundary conditions, the earlier evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In a single‐phase high-entropy alloy (HEA) that is not based on the traditional Nb–Ta or Ti-rich heavy transition metal systems, the superconducting transition temperature (Tc) is primarily governed by the degree of atomic-scale lattice distortion. A moderate increase in atomic size mismatch among the constituent elements will enhance electron–phonon coupling (by softening selected phonon modes), thereby raising Tc, whereas excessive lattice distortion introduces pair‐breaking scattering and suppresses Tc.
generation.material_initial_state: A single‐phase, solid-solution HEA composed of at least five elements (each present at ≥5 at.%) with a BCC structure and a moderate atomic size mismatch that yields a baseline superconducting Tc (Tc0).
generation.intervention: Systematically modify the alloy chemistry by substituting one or more constituent elements with others of significantly different atomic radii (but similar valence electron count) so as to progressively increase the atomic size mismatch while preserving single-phase stability and similar electron count.
generation.conditions: Measurements conducted at low temperatures (down to 1.8 K or lower) in a controlled cryogenic environment; all samples are verified via XRD/TEM to remain single-phase (e.g., BCC) and free of secondary phases or clustering effects that could independently affect superconductivity.
generation.structural_mediator: The degree of lattice distortion (quantified by local bond-length variations and peak broadening in XRD) that originates from the atomic size disparity among the elements.
generation.mechanism: Lattice distortion alters the phonon spectrum by introducing a distribution of local vibrational modes. Moderate distortion enhances the electron–phonon coupling constant (λ) by softening certain phonon modes that facilitate Cooper pair formation, thereby increasing Tc. However, if the distortion becomes too severe, the resulting enhanced scattering acts as a pair breaker and reduces Tc.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline alloy, a series of alloys with incrementally increased atomic size mismatch will first show an increase in Tc (due to enhanced electron–phonon coupling) up to an optimal point, beyond which further mismatch causes a decline in Tc because of increased pair-breaking scattering.
generation.baseline: An equiatomic HEA with a balanced atomic size mismatch that is superconducting at a baseline Tc (Tc0), serving as the control for comparison.
generation.boundary: The alloy must remain a homogeneous single-phase solid solution (e.g., BCC) with all constituents present at ≥5 at.% and with nearly constant average valence electron count; the temperature range for superconductivity is assumed to be below approximately 20 K.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative effect on Tc and the optimal degree of lattice distortion required to maximize Tc are uncertain and would need to be established experimentally; additional complicating factors such as subtle short-range ordering may also modify the electron–phonon coupling.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one set using a baseline composition known to be superconducting with moderate atomic size mismatch, and a second set in which one or more elements are substituted by elements with larger (or smaller) atomic radii to deliberately increase (or decrease) the lattice distortion while keeping the overall valence electron count nearly constant. Verify via XRD and TEM that both sets maintain the same single-phase BCC structure. Then, measure the superconducting transition temperature (Tc) of each sample using four-probe resistivity and magnetic susceptibility measurements in a cryostat.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (to assess phase purity and quantify lattice strain/peak broadening)
Transmission electron microscopy (for local structural assessment)
Four-probe resistivity vs. temperature (to determine Tc onset and zero resistance)
Magnetic susceptibility vs. temperature (to corroborate superconducting transition)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the series of alloys with increased atomic size mismatch does not exhibit the predicted non-monotonic change in Tc (i.e., an initial increase followed by a decrease beyond an optimal distortion) relative to the baseline, or if Tc remains unchanged or changes in a manner inconsistent with the hypothesis, then the hypothesis is falsified.
